{"content": "# ICTS CASE 2026-0412 — RECOMMENDED MEASURES
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HK-listed Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC, SEHK 2513) — GLM-family models
**Companion product:** OICTS Assessment, ICTS Case 2026-0412 ([assessment.md](./assessment.md))
**Authority:** E.O. 13873, as amended; 15 CFR part 791 (§§ 791.1, 791.7, 791.100–110); Entity List per 15 CFR 744, supplement no. 4; IEEPA authorities delegated to the Secretary
**Recommendation:** Adopt measures M2–M6 immediately as a package; retain M1 and M7–M9 as the supporting baseline. Do not adopt M-limitless (blanket possession ban) — see final paragraph. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.

---

**M1. Monitoring and intelligence baseline (retain under all options).** OICTS keeps Case 2026-0412 open, obtains the ODNI classified annex, and stands up quarterly reporting on GLM/Z.ai US exposure (API call volume by sector, marketplace availability, new GLM releases, enterprise-integration discoveries via SBOM sampling), while DHS/CISA issues a public advisory to critical-infrastructure operators describing the risk classes of foreign-adversary-derived AI models. Trade-off: this is the floor, not the policy — it preserves visibility and open-source research access at zero economic cost but changes nothing about the channels themselves, and GLM compounds into US infrastructure while we watch. Recommended as the intelligence baseline that runs underneath every other measure, not as a terminal response.

**M2. Federal-sector prohibition with contractor flow-down (implement immediately).** CISA and OMB issue guidance prohibiting the acquisition or use of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family models (hosted, marketplace, or self-hosted) on federal information systems, including government-furnished equipment, in the pattern already set by the DeepSeek device bans; OMB ties the restriction into M-25-21/22 implementation; a FAR case rule (with DFARS companion) prohibits foreign-adversary-derived AI components in contractor deliverables to USG, closing the "41 US products / six federal contractors" channel; DoD issues a service-wide direction on open weights per OUSD(I&S)'s input, covering downloaded weights on DoD networks and personally owned devices used for DoD work; OICTS supports pending No Adversarial AI Act legislation. Trade-off: immediately implementable and near-zero litigation risk for the government-use prong, but it protects only the federal ecosystem — the 2,300-organization commercial exposure and the general developer market remain untouched, and the FAR rule needs a rulemaking cycle.

**M3. Entity List consolidation — close the rebrand and evasion gaps (implement immediately).** Refer to the ERC additions of (i) Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited (the HK-listed parent, SEHK 2513), (ii) Jingsheng Hengxing Technology PTE. LTD (Singapore, the international service front), and (iii) all post-January-2025 subsidiaries and aliases (e.g., Zhejiang Zhipu Xinbian, the February 2025 Hangzhou subsidiary), under the same §744.11 military-modernization basis and presumption of denial as the ten existing entries; refer to Treasury for analysis of US institutional holdings in SEHK 2513 and for payments screening of the Singapore entity. Trade-off: low cost and closes the most obvious evasion route (the 2025 rebrand and the Singapore front were almost certainly built for this purpose), but Entity List controls the flow of items *to* Zhipu — they do not stop US persons *using* Zhipu services, since services are not EAR items. Necessary, not sufficient.

**M4. ICTS determination: prohibit US-person transactions involving Zhipu-hosted model services (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a §791.7 determination that the acquisition or use by US persons of hosted model services from Zhipu, Z.ai, or affiliates (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4, and successor endpoints) presents an undue risk to US national security, and prohibits those transactions, with enforcement directed at identifiable intermediaries — payment processors, US access points, the service entities' US commercial presence — rather than at individual subscribers, and with a 60–90 day wind-down for current subscribers to migrate. Trade-off: this closes the acute channel through which ~2,300 US-origin organizations are sending prompts, source code, and business documents to an Entity-Listed, intelligence-law-subject vendor; it will draw litigation (the IEEPA record under part 791 is strong but untested on AI services), imposes real migration costs on current users, and carries retaliation risk — none of which changes the underlying fact that this channel is the single highest-value exposure in the case.

**M5. ICTS determination: prohibit US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM open weights, absent negotiated mitigation (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a companion class-based determination that US persons may not distribute, host, serve, market, update, or otherwise deal in GLM-family artifacts originating from Zhipu or its affiliates — model hubs (e.g., the zai-org organization on Hugging Face), cloud marketplaces and inference providers (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita, Parasail, Baseten, OpenRouter-listed providers, and successors), and app stores for Z.ai applications — without an approved mitigation agreement, with takedown and user-notice obligations attached. This is deliberately aimed at the on-ramps, not at possession: files already downloaded remain where they are, offline mirrors remain outside US jurisdiction, and no individual is penalized for a past download. Trade-off: enforceable because every named intermediary is a US person with US nexus, and class-based prohibition has precedent in part 791 itself (the connected-vehicles rule); but it cannot reach what is already in the wild, it will be attacked rhetorically as "an open-source ban" (it is a country-of-origin distribution control on one vendor's artifacts), and it costs the United States some independent security-research visibility into GLM — mitigated by the M6 carve-out.

**M6. Narrow, revocable mitigation exception for intermediaries and researchers (adopt alongside M4–M5).** Where a US intermediary or an accredited research institution can demonstrate independent control — verified provenance and checksummed release lineage, third-party artifact scanning under the emerging white-box methods, AI bill-of-materials (AIBOM) disclosure, country-of-origin labeling in model cards and SBOMs, defined takedown obligations, and no commercial relationship with Zhipu or its affiliates — OICTS may permit continued hosting or research use under written conditions revocable at any time. Trade-off: preserves US infrastructure choice, keeps the research carve-out that makes M5 defensible, and transfers compliance cost to the distributor; the risk is that verification technology is immature (artifact methods cannot prove absence of poisoning today), so conditions must be treated as provisional and reviewed quarterly, and the exception must remain narrow enough that it does not become a paper regime.

**M7. Disclosure and labeling duties for the enterprise-integration channel (implement immediately).** Commerce (OICTS with NIST) publishes a requirement — first as guidance, then by rulemaking — that vendors of software and AI-enabled services sold in the US disclose foreign-adversary-derived model components (base or fine-tune) in AIBOMs/SBOMs, with specific mandatory disclosure to federal buyers and to critical-infrastructure customers, enforced by FTC/Commerce against undisclosed use; buyers' contracts should require flow-down of the same disclosure. Trade-off: this is the only tool that reaches the quiet channel — GLM embedded in products whose buyers never chose a Chinese model — and it is cheap and standards-friendly; its limits are that disclosure is not prohibition, enforcement against a disclosure failure is after the fact, and it depends on vendor honesty absent audit.

**M8. Critical-infrastructure and sector-regulator actions (implement on the same schedule as M2).** Sector regulators and CISA advise — and where statutory authority exists, require — the exclusion of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family self-hosted deployments from systems that operate or are connected to critical infrastructure (energy, financial services, water, communications, healthcare), in line with CISA's supply-chain concern that open-weight backdoors and poisoning cannot be ruled out; regulators (FERC/NERC, financial regulators, HHS) incorporate the prohibition into their inspection regimes. Trade-off: this is where private self-hosted use is both visible and governable, so it substitutes for an unenforceable blanket ban (see below) without leaving a gap for the highest-consequence deployments; the cost is regulator-by-regulator implementation time and compliance burden on operators.

**M9. Allied engagement and retaliation contingency (State/EB lead; begin now).** State briefs allies and partner governments on the Zhipu case file — sovereign-AI customers along the Belt and Road are the intended audience of our evidence on Huawei-based "AI-in-a-box," joint innovation centers, and standards capture — and coordinates reciprocal measures; Treasury, Commerce, and USTR jointly model and prepare mitigation for PRC retaliation against US firms with China exposure (Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, US AI labs' partners), including export-licensing flexibility and market-access remedies. Trade-off: early engagement raises the cost of Beijing flipping our measures into a "tech hegemony" narrative and multiplies the effect by closing third markets to Zhipu's sovereign-AI play; the risk is that allies move at different speeds and leaks complicate the interagency process. Not doing it concedes the third-world standards contest that is the actual prize.

**Not recommended: a blanket prohibition on possession or private offline use of GLM weights.** State/EB's objection is sustained: such a ban would be novel (the first US prohibition on mere possession of software), unenforceable against private servers, offshore mirrors, and already-downloaded files, and maximally provocative, and it would undercut the enforceable architecture above by attaching the whole policy to its weakest link. The recommended package (M2–M6, with M7–M9 in support) covers every channel that the US Government can actually see and compel — hosted services, distribution intermediaries, federal procurement, critical infrastructure, and disclosure — which is where the risk actually lives.

---

*Prepared by the OICTS Analytic Cell, October 2026. Case material CUI//PROPIN — do not reproduce outside the enclave. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.*

**— END MEASURES —**

3. **The Tsinghua military-civil fusion nexus.** Zhipu's founding lab sits inside the university that is among China's top civilian awardees of AI-related defense contracts ([CSET](https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/pulling-back-the-curtain-on-chinas-military-civil-fusion/)) and whose leadership has publicly committed to supporting the national military-civil fusion and AI-superpower strategies ([CNAS translation of Tsinghua VP You Zheng](https://www.cnas.org/publications/commentary/tsinghuas-approach-to-military-civil-fusion-in-artificial-intelligence)). The Entity List rationale ("development and integration of advanced AI research") maps directly onto this institutional reality.
4. **PRC government procurement.** Zhipu won 12 of 81 state-sector LLM contracts in H1 2024 — more than any other vendor ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3267866/chinas-public-sector-accelerates-ai-adoption-2024-zhipu-and-iflytek-emerge-winners); [QQ/骑牛研究所](https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20240626A00GFL00)); a RMB 61.28M Hangzhou municipal deal in May 2025 ([Wikipedia/SCMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)); and a RMB 10.9M China Meteorological Administration contract signed 10 March 2026 for a severe-weather LLM warning platform ([ccgp via 163.com](https://www.163.com/dy/article/KNSSN7E705562DGT.html)). State revenue is structural, not incidental.
5. **Party-state engagement and standards.** Leadership engages Premier Li Qiang; the company plays an active role in setting national AI technical standards ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)).
6. **Digital Silk Road execution.** Sovereign-LLM infrastructure, Huawei "AI-in-a-box," joint innovation centers and national-LLM co-builds across ASEAN, the Gulf, and Africa; Gulf sovereign-capital participation; Huawei Ascend compatibility announced August 2025 ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)).
7. **Ecosystem capture.** The RMB 300M "Z Fund" finances open-source AI projects worldwide, explicitly not limited to Zhipu models ([21jingji](https://www.21jingji.com/article/20250418/herald/a0f8f199cdf330c1ab8e6f18e7e586a2.html)) — a subsidy program for dependency formation, run by an Entity-Listed company.

**Assessment.** We assess with high confidence that Zhipu's ties to the PRC state and military ecosystem are definitional rather than incidental, and that "arms-length commercial vendor" is not an available characterization of this company. The open question is not the relationship; it is the operational use Beijing makes of Zhipu's foreign channels — which is precisely where our collection is thinnest (see Intelligence Gaps and the ODNI classified annex).

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HK-listed as Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited, SEHK 2513) — GLM-family large language models
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell (draft for interagency review — DoD, DHS, ODNI, State, Treasury)
**Decision authority:** Executive Director, OICTS; Under Secretary. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.
**Date:** October 2026 (COB Friday suspense). Handling: case material is CUI//PROPIN; do not reproduce outside the enclave.
**Transaction classes under review:** (a) US persons' use of Z.ai hosted API services (api.z.ai; open.bigmodel.cn; api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4); (b) distribution of open GLM weights through US-based model hubs and cloud marketplaces; (c) integration of GLM models into US enterprise products. These fall within the "acquisition, importation, transfer, installation, dealing in, or use of" ICTS by a person "owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of" a foreign adversary within the meaning of E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR part 791 ([eCFR 15 CFR 791.1](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-15/subtitle-B/chapter-VII/subchapter-E/part-791)).

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is not a commercial AI vendor that happens to be Chinese; it is a PRC state-aligned instrument executing Beijing's AI strategy, and its GLM models are already a working component of the US software stack. Three facts drive this assessment. First, on 16 January 2025 the End-User Review Committee placed Zhipu and nine affiliates on the Entity List with a presumption of denial because they "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research" — the US Government's own determination that Zhipu is a military-relevant actor ([90 FR 4617](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00704/addition-of-entities-to-and-revision-of-entry-on-the-entity-list); [BIS press release](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security)). Second, Zhipu is among the most heavily state-capitalized AI developers in China — more than $1.4 billion in state-backed investment by OpenAI's assessment, including roughly RMB 2 billion (US$280M) of local-government capital in 2025 alone — with leadership that engages Premier Li Qiang, a role in drafting PRC national AI standards, and an export strategy that packages sovereign LLM infrastructure and Huawei Ascend-based "AI-in-a-box" for governments along the Belt and Road ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/); [21jingji](https://www.21jingji.com/article/20250418/herald/a0f8f199cdf330c1ab8e6f18e7e586a2.html)). Third, US exposure is no longer hypothetical: approximately 2,300 US-origin organizations called Z.ai hosted endpoints in Q3 2026 (case data, low precision); GLM weights have accumulated millions of downloads and are served by at least nine US inference providers and marketplaces; and GLM appears embedded in 41 US software products, six of them federal contractors (case data).

**Recommendation: this case is not a candidate for watchful waiting.** The threat standard under E.O. 13873 is "undue or unacceptable risk," not proof of malice, and that standard is already met by an Entity-Listed, state-funded, intelligence-law-subject vendor controlling a channel through which thousands of US organizations send prompts, source code, and business documents. We recommend prohibition-class ICTS determinations against the two highest-risk channels — Zhipu-hosted API services, and US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM weights — combined with an immediate federal-sector prohibition with contractor flow-down, Entity List consolidation covering the rebranded Hong Kong parent and the Singapore service front, and enforceable disclosure duties for the enterprise-integration channel. A ban on private, offline self-hosting of already-downloaded weights should be deferred on enforceability grounds — not because the risk is lower. Full measures and trade-offs below and at [measures.md](./measures.md).

---

*Confidence levels per ICD 203: confidence characterizes the evidentiary basis for a judgment; likelihood terms (e.g., "very likely") characterize the probability of the event or development.*

**KJ-1 (High confidence). Zhipu operates as an instrument of PRC state strategy, and its corporate identity is inseparable from Beijing's goals.** Zhipu was founded in 2019 as a Tsinghua University spin-out (the "sister organization to a top Chinese academic computer science lab," per [Bismarck Brief](https://brief.bismarckanalysis.com/p/ai-2026-zai-is-open-to-government)), was recapitalized in 2024–25 with Saudi and PRC state funds, listed in Hong Kong on 8 January 2026 as Knowledge Atlas Technology (SEHK 2513, [HKEX filings](https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0107/2026010701798.pdf)), and is now China's most valuable listed AI pure play (~US$62B market cap as of August 2026, [Wikipedia/Z.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)). Its chairman publicly frames the mission as contributing "China's AI power to the world" ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)). We assess with high confidence that Zhipu's autonomy from the Party-state is nominal: the funding, the standards role, the procurement base, and the leadership's own positioning all run one direction.

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

Ordered from least to most restrictive; trade-offs stated. Full text of recommendations at [measures.md](./measures.md).

**Option 1 — Monitoring only.** Continue OICTS investigation; obtain the ODNI classified annex; quarterly exposure reporting; CISA advisory. *Pros:* zero economic disruption, preserves open-source norms and security-research access. *Cons:* concedes every channel identified above while GLM compounds into infrastructure; no deterrent; incompatible with an Entity List determination already on the books. **Not recommended as a terminal state.** Retain as the intelligence baseline under any other option.

**Option 2 — Federal-sector prohibition and procurement controls.** CISA/OMB guidance prohibiting Z.ai services and GLM-family use on federal systems; FAR case rule with flow-down to contractors; support for the pending No Adversarial AI Act ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-lawmakers-introduce-bill-bar-chinese-ai-us-government-agencies-2025-06-25/)); department-level device bans in the Commerce/DeepSeek pattern ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-commerce-department-bureaus-ban-chinas-deepseek-government-devices-sources-2025-03-17/)); OMB M-25-21/22 implementation ([White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2025/04/white-house-releases-new-policies-on-federal-agency-ai-use-and-procurement/)). *Pros:* immediately implementable; addresses DoD's network concern; closes the 41-products/six-contractors channel for the federal ecosystem. *Cons:* leaves the commercial sector and state/local untouched; depends on enforcement capacity; does not touch the hosted API used by the private sector.

**Option 3 — Entity List consolidation.** ERC action to add the Hong Kong-listed parent (Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC), the Singapore service entity (Jingsheng Hengxing), and post-January 2025 subsidiaries and aliases; Treasury referral for capital-flow and payments screening. *Pros:* closes the rebrand gap and the obvious evasion route; low direct cost. *Cons:* EAR controls exports *to* Zhipu; it does not stop US persons *using* Zhipu services, which are not EAR items. Necessary but not sufficient.

**Option 4 — ICTS determination prohibiting the hosted-API channel.** Determine under 15 CFR 791.7 that US persons' acquisition or use of Zhipu/Z.ai hosted model services (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, coding endpoints) presents an undue risk, and prohibit it. *Pros:* eliminates the acute data channel — the single highest-value exposure (~2,300 organizations) — and is enforceable against identifiable intermediaries: payment rails, US access points, and the service entity's US commercial presence. *Cons:* migration burden for current users; will be litigated; retaliation risk (see below).

**Option 5 — ICTS determination prohibiting US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM weights.** Determine that US-based model hubs, cloud marketplaces, infer
... [3542 chars truncated] ...
ERC, financial, health-sector regulators), and disclosure duties (Option 6-style AIBOM requirements) — rather than by a criminal prohibition the government cannot police.

**Reciprocity and retaliation (State/EB).** PRC retaliation is a real cost but not a new one: Beijing already excludes US models and US hardware from state procurement, and US firms with major PRC exposure (Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, US AI labs' partners) are already exposed. The measures above take aim at *channels*, not at PRC persons generally, and mirror restrictions Beijing already imposes on US ICTS. We assess the marginal retaliation risk of Options 2–5 as low to moderate, and the strategic cost of inaction as high: the PRC's stated objective — captured in Zhipu's own positioning — is to lock Chinese AI systems and standards into as many markets as possible before the West organizes ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)).

---

## Intelligence Gaps

1. **Covert content of GLM weights.** We cannot confirm or rule out trigger-conditioned behaviors, poisoning, or sleeper constructs in any GLM release with existing methods; GLM-specific deep evaluation is thinner than DeepSeek's ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). This gap is not closeable by analysis; it requires sustained artifact research (recommend funding a NIST/CAISI GLM evaluation).
2. **Actual data flows of the hosted channel.** No visibility into whether US-person API traffic is wholly processed in Singapore or transits mainland infrastructure; no visibility into PRC state requests to Zhipu or its affiliates. The ODNI classified annex (available on request; not in this enclave) may partially address this.
3. **Zhipu–PLA operational nexus.** The ERC determination and Recorded Future's assessment establish the military-modernization link; specific projects, contracts, or tasking involving Zhipu models in PLA systems are not visible in open sources.
4. **Hong Kong/Singapore structure.** Full shareholder table and control chain of the listed parent (including any post-IPO state-linked stakes) requires the HKEX prospectus and Treasury analysis; Treasury/OIA input is still pending (interagency input).
5. **Exposure precision.** The ~2,300-organization estimate is low-precision CDN telemetry; the identity of the 41 US products and the six federal contractors, and what data those products transmit, remain unenumerated (case data). SBOM sampling does not capture silent dependencies.
6. **US institutional capital exposure.** US persons can and likely do hold SEHK 2513 shares; scale unknown.
7. **PRC retaliation planning and allied positions.** No collection reflected in this product; State/EB and ODNI inputs needed before final decision.
8. **Update-channel telemetry.** No visibility into how often GLM repositories issue config/tokenizer/code updates to already-downloaded weights, or who consumes them.

# ICTS CASE 2026-0412 — RECOMMENDED MEASURES
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HK-listed Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC, SEHK 2513) — GLM-family models
**Companion product:** OICTS Assessment, ICTS Case 2026-0412 ([assessment.md](./assessment.md))
**Authority:** E.O. 13873, as amended; 15 CFR part 791 (§§ 791.1, 791.7, 791.100–110); Entity List per 15 CFR 744, supplement no. 4; IEEPA authorities delegated to the Secretary
**Recommendation:** Adopt measures M2–M6 immediately as a package; retain M1 and M7–M9 as the supporting baseline. Do not adopt M-limitless (blanket possession ban) — see final paragraph. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.

---

**M1. Monitoring and intelligence baseline (retain under all options).** OICTS keeps Case 2026-0412 open, obtains the ODNI classified annex, and stands up quarterly reporting on GLM/Z.ai US exposure (API call volume by sector, marketplace availability, new GLM releases, enterprise-integration discoveries via SBOM sampling), while DHS/CISA issues a public advisory to critical-infrastructure operators describing the risk classes of foreign-adversary-derived AI models. Trade-off: this is the floor, not the policy — it preserves visibility and open-source research access at zero economic cost but changes nothing about the channels themselves, and GLM compounds into US infrastructure while we watch. Recommended as the intelligence baseline that runs underneath every other measure, not as a terminal response.

**M2. Federal-sector prohibition with contractor flow-down (implement immediately).** CISA and OMB issue guidance prohibiting the acquisition or use of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family models (hosted, marketplace, or self-hosted) on federal information systems, including government-furnished equipment, in the pattern already set by the DeepSeek device bans; OMB ties the restriction into M-25-21/22 implementation; a FAR case rule (with DFARS companion) prohibits foreign-adversary-derived AI components in contractor deliverables to USG, closing the "41 US products / six federal contractors" channel; DoD issues a service-wide direction on open weights per OUSD(I&S)'s input, covering downloaded weights on DoD networks and personally owned devices used for DoD work; OICTS supports pending No Adversarial AI Act legislation. Trade-off: immediately implementable and near-zero litigation risk for the government-use prong, but it protects only the federal ecosystem — the 2,300-organization commercial exposure and the general developer market remain untouched, and the FAR rule needs a rulemaking cycle.

**M3. Entity List consolidation — close the rebrand and evasion gaps (implement immediately).** Refer to the ERC additions of (i) Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited (the HK-listed parent, SEHK 2513), (ii) Jingsheng Hengxing Technology PTE. LTD (Singapore, the international service front), and (iii) all post-January-2025 subsidiaries and aliases (e.g., Zhejiang Zhipu Xinbian, the February 2025 Hangzhou subsidiary), under the same §744.11 military-modernization basis and presumption of denial as the ten existing entries; refer to Treasury for analysis of US institutional holdings in SEHK 2513 and for payments screening of the Singapore entity. Trade-off: low cost and closes the most obvious evasion route (the 2025 rebrand and the Singapore front were almost certainly built for this purpose), but Entity List controls the flow of items *to* Zhipu — they do not stop US persons *using* Zhipu services, since services are not EAR items. Necessary, not sufficient.

**M4. ICTS determination: prohibit US-person transactions involving Zhipu-hosted model services (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a §791.7 determination that the acquisition or use by US persons of hosted model services from Zhipu, Z.ai, or affiliates (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4, and successor endpoints) presents an undue risk to US national security, and prohibits those transactions, with enforcement directed at identifiable intermediaries — payment processors, US access points, the service entities' US commercial presence — rather than at individual subscribers, and with a 60–90 day wind-down for current subscribers to migrate. Trade-off: this closes the acute channel through which ~2,300 US-origin organizations are sending prompts, source code, and business documents to an Entity-Listed, intelligence-law-subject vendor; it will draw litigation (the IEEPA record under part 791 is strong but untested on AI services), imposes real migration costs on current users, and carries retaliation risk — none of which changes the underlying fact that this channel is the single highest-value exposure in the case.

**M5. ICTS determination: prohibit US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM open weights, absent negotiated mitigation (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a companion class-based determination that US persons may not distribute, host, serve, market, update, or otherwise deal in GLM-family artifacts originating from Zhipu or its affiliates — model hubs (e.g., the zai-org organization on Hugging Face), cloud marketplaces and inference providers (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita, Parasail, Baseten, OpenRouter-listed providers, and successors), and app stores for Z.ai applications — without an approved mitigation agreement, with takedown and user-notice obligations attached. This is deliberately aimed at the on-ramps, not at possession: files already downloaded remain where they are, offline mirrors remain outside US jurisdiction, and no individual is penalized for a past download. Trade-off: enforceable because every named intermediary is a US person with US nexus, and class-based prohibition has precedent in part 791 itself (the connected-vehicles rule); but it cannot reach what is already in the wild, it will be attacked rhetorically as "an open-source ban" (it is a country-of-origin distribution control on one vendor's artifacts), and it costs the United States some independent security-research visibility into GLM — mitigated by the M6 carve-out.

**M6. Narrow, revocable mitigation exception for intermediaries and researchers (adopt alongside M4–M5).** Where a US intermediary or an accredited research institution can demonstrate independent control — verified provenance and checksummed release lineage, third-party artifact scanning under the emerging white-box methods, AI bill-of-materials (AIBOM) disclosure, country-of-origin labeling in model cards and SBOMs, defined takedown obligations, and no commercial relationship with Zhipu or its affiliates — OICTS may permit continued hosting or research use under written conditions revocable at any time. Trade-off: preserves US infrastructure choice, keeps the research carve-out that makes M5 defensible, and transfers compliance cost to the distributor; the risk is that verification technology is immature (artifact methods cannot prove absence of poisoning today), so conditions must be treated as provisional and reviewed quarterly, and the exception must remain narrow enough that it does not become a paper regime.

**M7. Disclosure and labeling duties for the enterprise-integration channel (implement immediately).** Commerce (OICTS with NIST) publishes a requirement — first as guidance, then by rulemaking — that vendors of software and AI-enabled services sold in the US disclose foreign-adversary-derived model components (base or fine-tune) in AIBOMs/SBOMs, with specific mandatory disclosure to federal buyers and to critical-infrastructure customers, enforced by FTC/Commerce against undisclosed use; buyers' contracts should require flow-down of the same disclosure. Trade-off: this is the only tool that reaches the quiet channel — GLM embedded in products whose buyers never chose a Chinese model — and it is cheap and standards-friendly; its limits are that disclosure is not prohibition, enforcement against a disclosure failure is after the fact, and it depends on vendor honesty absent audit.

**M8. Critical-infrastructure and sector-regulator actions (implement on the same schedule as M2).** Sector regulators and CISA advise — and where statutory authority exists, require — the exclusion of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family self-hosted deployments from systems that operate or are connected to critical infrastructure (energy, financial services, water, communications, healthcare), in line with CISA's supply-chain concern that open-weight backdoors and poisoning cannot be ruled out; regulators (FERC/NERC, financial regulators, HHS) incorporate the prohibition into their inspection regimes. Trade-off: this is where private self-hosted use is both visible and governable, so it substitutes for an unenforceable blanket ban (see below) without leaving a gap for the highest-consequence deployments; the cost is regulator-by-regulator implementation time and compliance burden on operators.

**M9. Allied engagement and retaliation contingency (State/EB lead; begin now).** State briefs allies and partner governments on the Zhipu case file — sovereign-AI customers along the Belt and Road are the intended audience of our evidence on Huawei-based "AI-in-a-box," joint innovation centers, and standards capture — and coordinates reciprocal measures; Treasury, Commerce, and USTR jointly model and prepare mitigation for PRC retaliation against US firms with China exposure (Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, US AI labs' partners), including export-licensing flexibility and market-access remedies. Trade-off: early engagement raises the cost of Beijing flipping our measures into a "tech hegemony" narrative and multiplies the effect by closing third markets to Zhipu's sovereign-AI play; the risk is that allies move at different speeds and leaks complicate the interagency process. Not doing it concedes the third-world standards contest that is the actual prize.

**Not recommended: a blanket prohibition on possession or private offline use of GLM weights.** State/EB's objection is sustained: such a ban would be novel (the first US prohibition on mere possession of software), unenforceable against private servers, offshore mirrors, and already-downloaded files, and maximally provocative, and it would undercut the enforceable architecture above by attaching the whole policy to its weakest link. The recommended package (M2–M6, with M7–M9 in support) covers every channel that the US Government can actually see and compel — hosted services, distribution intermediaries, federal procurement, critical infrastructure, and disclosure — which is where the risk actually lives.

---

*Prepared by the OICTS Analytic Cell, October 2026. Case material CUI//PROPIN — do not reproduce outside the enclave. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.*

**— END MEASURES —**
Step budget exhausted; episode closing.

# OICTS ASSESSMENT — ICTS Case 2026-0412
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HK-listed as Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited, SEHK 2513) — GLM-family large language models
**Prepared by:** OICTS Analytic Cell (draft for interagency review — DoD, DHS, ODNI, State, Treasury)
**Decision authority:** Executive Director, OICTS; Under Secretary. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.
**Date:** October 2026 (COB Friday suspense). Handling: case material is CUI//PROPIN; do not reproduce outside the enclave.
**Transaction classes under review:** (a) US persons' use of Z.ai hosted API services (api.z.ai; open.bigmodel.cn; api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4); (b) distribution of open GLM weights through US-based model hubs and cloud marketplaces; (c) integration of GLM models into US enterprise products. These fall within the "acquisition, importation, transfer, installation, dealing in, or use of" ICTS by a person "owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction of" a foreign adversary within the meaning of E.O. 13873 and 15 CFR part 791 ([eCFR 15 CFR 791.1](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-15/subtitle-B/chapter-VII/subchapter-E/part-791)).

---

## Bottom Line Up Front

Zhipu AI is not a commercial AI vendor that happens to be Chinese; it is a PRC state-aligned instrument executing Beijing's AI strategy, and its GLM models are already a working component of the US software stack. Three facts drive this assessment. First, on 16 January 2025 the End-User Review Committee placed Zhipu and nine affiliates on the Entity List with a presumption of denial because they "advance the People's Republic of China's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research" — the US Government's own determination that Zhipu is a military-relevant actor ([90 FR 4617](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00704/addition-of-entities-to-and-revision-of-entry-on-the-entity-list); [BIS press release](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security)). Second, Zhipu is among the most heavily state-capitalized AI developers in China — more than $1.4 billion in state-backed investment by OpenAI's assessment, including roughly RMB 2 billion (US$280M) of local-government capital in 2025 alone — with leadership that engages Premier Li Qiang, a role in drafting PRC national AI standards, and an export strategy that packages sovereign LLM infrastructure and Huawei Ascend-based "AI-in-a-box" for governments along the Belt and Road ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/); [21jingji](https://www.21jingji.com/article/20250418/herald/a0f8f199cdf330c1ab8e6f18e7e586a2.html)). Third, US exposure is no longer hypothetical: approximately 2,300 US-origin organizations called Z.ai hosted endpoints in Q3 2026 (case data, low precision); GLM weights have accumulated millions of downloads and are served by at least nine US inference providers and marketplaces; and GLM appears embedded in 41 US software products, six of them federal contractors (case data).

**Recommendation: this case is not a candidate for watchful waiting.** The threat standard under E.O. 13873 is "undue or unacceptable risk," not proof of malice, and that standard is already met by an Entity-Listed, state-funded, intelligence-law-subject vendor controlling a channel through which thousands of US organizations send prompts, source code, and business documents. We recommend prohibition-class ICTS determinations against the two highest-risk channels — Zhipu-hosted API services, and US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM weights — combined with an immediate federal-sector prohibition with contractor flow-down, Entity List consolidation covering the rebranded Hong Kong parent and the Singapore service front, and enforceable disclosure duties for the enterprise-integration channel. A ban on private, offline self-hosting of already-downloaded weights should be deferred on enforceability grounds — not because the risk is lower. Full measures and trade-offs below and at [measures.md](./measures.md).

---

## Key Judgments

*Confidence levels per ICD 203: confidence characterizes the evidentiary basis for a judgment; likelihood terms (e.g., "very likely") characterize the probability of the event or development.*

**KJ-1 (High confidence). Zhipu operates as an instrument of PRC state strategy, and its corporate identity is inseparable from Beijing's goals.** Zhipu was founded in 2019 as a Tsinghua University spin-out (the "sister organization to a top Chinese academic computer science lab," per [Bismarck Brief](https://brief.bismarckanalysis.com/p/ai-2026-zai-is-open-to-government)), was recapitalized in 2024–25 with Saudi and PRC state funds, listed in Hong Kong on 8 January 2026 as Knowledge Atlas Technology (SEHK 2513, [HKEX filings](https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0107/2026010701798.pdf)), and is now China's most valuable listed AI pure play (~US$62B market cap as of August 2026, [Wikipedia/Z.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)). Its chairman publicly frames the mission as contributing "China's AI power to the world" ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)). We assess with high confidence that Zhipu's autonomy from the Party-state is nominal: the funding, the standards role, the procurement base, and the leadership's own positioning all run one direction.

**KJ-2 (High confidence in the USG determination; moderate confidence in the specific corroboration). Zhipu advances PRC military modernization.** The ERC determination of 16 January 2025 under §744.11 is the authoritative USG judgment ([90 FR 4617](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00704/addition-of-entities-to-and-revision-of-entry-on-the-entity-list); [BIS](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security)). Open-source corroboration is strong but indirect: Recorded Future assesses with high confidence ("very likely") that PLA units and PRC defense industry have used domestic LLMs — explicitly including Zhipu AI — to build generative-AI intelligence tools, with PLA patent applications for OSINT-generation systems ([Recorded Future, "Artificial Eyes"](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence)); Tsinghua, the parent institution of Zhipu's founders, is a top awardee of AI-related defense contracts and has publicly committed to military-civil fusion in AI ([CSET](https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/pulling-back-the-curtain-on-chinas-military-civil-fusion/); [CNAS](https://www.cnas.org/publications/commentary/tsinghuas-approach-to-military-civil-fusion-in-artificial-intelligence)). We have no public evidence that any released GLM weight file is used inside a PLA weapons system; the military-modernization nexus runs through research collaboration and ecosystem integration, which is exactly what the ERC found.

**KJ-3 (High confidence). Zhipu is executing Beijing's "Digital Silk Road" — sovereign-AI export to third governments — and is winning.** OpenAI analysts assess Zhipu is offering "China's answer to OpenAI for Countries": sovereign LLM infrastructure, turnkey Huawei "AI-in-a-box" hardware, joint innovation centers and national-LLM co-builds across Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Kenya, plus a Dubai content-safety lab, Gulf capital participation (Prosperity7/Aramco), and Huawei Ascend hardware ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/)). The stated goal is to lock Chinese systems and standards into emerging markets before US or European rivals can. This is the strategy of the PRC state, executed through Zhipu; it is not a private go-to-market plan.

**KJ-4 (Moderate-to-high confidence). US-person data in the hosted-API channel is presumptively accessible to PRC state organs, regardless of the Singapore front and contractual zero-retention claims.** The international Z.ai service is operated by Jingsheng Hengxing Technology PTE. LTD (Singapore), a PRC-parent affiliate, while the mainland endpoint (open.bigmodel.cn) hosts data in China ([Z.ai Privacy Policy](https://docs.z.ai/legal-agreement/privacy-policy); [API privacy comparison](https://erkinekici.com/articles/comparing-llm-api-privacy/)). PRC law — National Intelligence Law Art. 7 and 14, Cybersecurity Law Art. 37, Data Security Law, Counter-Espionage Law as amended — obliges and empowers state organs to demand cooperation from PRC organizations ([NPC text](http://www.npc.gov.cn/zgrdw/npc/xinwen/2017-06/27/content_2024529.htm); [China Law Translate](https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/en/national-intelligence-law-of-the-p-r-c-2017/)). No contractual term of a Singapore subsidiary can displace the law governing its parent. We cannot confirm actual data flows (gap), but the burden of proof should not rest on the US Government.

**KJ-5 (High confidence in the structural risk; the presence or absence of covert technical behavior in GLM weights cannot be confirmed with existing methods). Open-weight distribution is the largest and least-governable exposure channel.** DHS/CISA reports no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights to date (interagency input), and independent research has found no demonstrated trigger-conditioned backdoor in any released Chinese open-weight model ([Anthony West, "Security Research into Chinese Open-Weight Models"](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). That is a statement about the state of testing, not about the models: artifact-level methods cannot reconstruct a training set, identify an unknown trigger, or prove the absence of poisoning; scanning for sleeper-agent behavior is nascent ([Microsoft, Feb 2026](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/04/detecting-backdoored-language-models-at-scale/)); and GLM specifically has received thin model-specific security evaluation outside comparative cyber benchmarks ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). Once weights are distributed there is no provider-side monitoring, refusal preservation, or kill switch — and the MIT-style license under which GLM has shipped since 2025 is perpetual and irrevocable ([Z.ai GLM-5.3 license](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/raw/main/LICENSE); [Wikipedia/Z.ai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)). The structural risk does not depend on covert behavior being found.

**KJ-6 (High confidence in direction; magnitude is low-precision). US exposure is material, distributed, and accelerating.** Roughly 2,300 US-origin organizations called Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (case data; CDN telemetry, low precision); GLM repositories show >9M cumulative downloads across all geographies (case data; [Hugging Face zai-org](https://huggingface.co/zai-org)); at least nine US inference providers and marketplaces serve GLM (case data; e.g., [Together](https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org), [Fireworks](https://fireworks.ai/models/fireworks/glm-4p6), [DeepInfra](https://deepinfra.com/zai-org/GLM-4.6)); 41 US software products embed GLM, six of them federal contractors (case data). Zhipu's own investor-relations team confirms the GLM Coding Plan user base is "primarily concentrated in the United States and China" ([Tech Buzz, Jan 2026](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/china-s-zhipu-ai-coding-agent-breaks-into-us-developer-market)). Adoption accelerated after the 12 June 2026 Commerce export-control action against US model providers made GLM the cheap substitute of choice ([Reuters](https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/anthropic-us-officials-meeting-monday-151958942.html); [altpaths](https://altpaths.io/news/3583)). Chinese-origin models, GLM prominent among them, now hold a visible share of US developer usage ([Al Jazeera, Nov 2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2025/11/13/chinas-ai-is-quietly-making-big-inroads-in-silicon-valley)).

**KJ-7 (Moderate confidence). Absent intervention, GLM becomes infrastructure-level US dependency within 12–24 months.** GLM-5.2 is within roughly a point of leading US models on key agentic benchmarks at a fraction of the cost ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/06/26/how-zai-is-closing-in-on-americas-ai-frontier.html); [altpaths](https://altpaths.io/news/3583)); the UK AI Security Institute measures the cyber-capability lag of leading open-weight models behind closed frontier systems at four-to-seven months ([Anthony West summary](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)); Zhipu's overseas paid base grew tenfold in two months on the strength of one release ([Asia Daily](https://asiadaily.org/news/9856/)). Cost-sensitive adoption compounds quietly: "Chinese open models have become a de facto standard among startups in the US" ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2025/11/13/chinas-ai-is-quietly-making-big-inroads-in-silicon-valley)). Every month of delay buys Zhipu network effects, developer habituation, and a standards beachhead it cannot easily be dislodged from later.

**KJ-8 (High confidence). The defensible legal architecture is prohibition at the distribution and service channels plus procurement controls — not bans on possession.** Section 791.1 covers acquisition, importation, transfer, installation, dealing in, and *use* of ICTS by or through US persons; the practical enforcement surface is the intermediaries — model hubs, cloud marketplaces, inference providers, app stores, payment rails — not the private server running an already-downloaded weight file (see Enforceability, below). Class-based prohibition has precedent in this very part ([15 CFR 791 subpart D, connected vehicles](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00592/securing-the-information-and-communications-technology-and-services-supply-chain-connected-vehicles)).

---

## Subject Overview (ownership, funding, leadership)

**Corporate identity.** Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd. was established 11 June 2019 and converted to a joint-stock company on 26 March 2025; its H shares listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on 8 January 2026 under the name Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited (SEHK 2513; offer price HK$116.20; 37.4M H shares) ([HKEX articles of association](https://www.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0107/2026010700005.pdf); [allotment results](https://www1.hkexnews.hk/listedco/listconews/sehk/2026/0107/2026010701798.pdf)). International branding changed from "Zhipu AI" to "Z.ai" in 2025 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)); the mainland product remains open.bigmodel.cn/zhipuai.cn. The rebrand has no substantive effect on control, and the Hong Kong parent and the Singapore service entity are not, on the public record, named in the January 2025 Entity List entries (see Intelligence Gaps).

**Founders and leadership.** The company is a Tsinghua University spin-out from the Knowledge Engineering Group (KEG): founders Tang Jie (chief scientist) and Li Juanzi are Tsinghua faculty; CEO Zhang Peng is a Tsinghua alumnus; Chairman Liu Debing runs capital operations ([Caixin profile, Jul 2026](https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-07-02/in-profile-this-trio-is-charting-the-course-for-chinas-leading-ai-developer-102460058.html); [Bismarck Brief](https://brief.bismarckanalysis.com/p/ai-2026-zai-is-open-to-government)). Tang Jie's team built the Wu Dao mega-models and the AMiner academic platform at Tsinghua ([Tsinghua](https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn/en/info/1418/10451.htm)). Headcount is ~500–800 ([Bismarck](https://brief.bismarckanalysis.com/p/ai-2026-zai-is-open-to-government); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)). Leadership engagement runs to the top of the Party-state, including Premier Li Qiang ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)).

**Funding.** Private Chinese capital came first (Alibaba, Tencent, Meituan, Ant, Xiaomi, HongShan, ~RMB 2.5B in 2023), followed by Saudi Prosperity7 in a ~US$400M round at ~US$3B valuation (May 2024) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)). Then the state arrived in force: in March 2025 alone, Hangzhou state capital (Hangzhou Municipal Construction Investment Group and Shangcheng Capital — both controlled by the Hangzhou government) participated in a >RMB 1B strategic round, Zhuhai Huafa Group added RMB 500M, and the Chengdu Hi-Tech Zone RMB 300M ([Reuters, 3 Mar 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinas-zhipu-ai-raises-137-million-state-funds-bet-ai-race-2025-03-03/); [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-03-03/alibaba-backed-zhipu-raises-140-million-as-deepseek-heats-up-ai); [Reuters, 19 Mar 2025](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-firm-zhipu-raises-257-mln-state-backed-funding-spree-2025-03-19/); [chnfund](https://www.chnfund.com/article/ARa30fdf29-a311-4df3-63bb-3a186bfa1f54)); the Beijing AI Industry Investment Fund added RMB 200M in April 2025 ([21jingji](https://www.21jingji.com/article/20250418/herald/a0f8f199cdf330c1ab8e6f18e7e586a2.html)), bringing 2025 local-government investment to ~RMB 2B (~US$280M). OpenAI assesses cumulative state-backed investment above US$1.4B ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)). In February 2025 Zhipu registered a wholly-owned Hangzhou subsidiary with RMB 450M registered capital ([chnfund](https://www.chnfund.com/article/ARa30fdf29-a311-4df3-63bb-3a186bfa1f54)) — a wholly-owned RMB 450M-registered vehicle created in Hangzhou weeks before the Hangzhou state-capital round was announced.

**Control assessment.** Between the state capital stack, the standards role, the procurement base, and the Party-state access of its leadership, we judge the "owned by, controlled by, or subject to the jurisdiction or direction" prong of E.O. 13873 to be comfortably satisfied as a matter of fact and law. The relevant question for policy is not *whether* Zhipu answers to Beijing, but *which* of its channels the US Government will continue to tolerate.

---

## Links to PRC Government / Military Entities

1. **USG determination — military modernization.** The ERC added ten Zhipu-affiliated entries — the Beijing parent, five Beijing affiliates (Lingxin, Yuanyin, Zhipu Future, Zhipu Linghang, Zhipu Qingyan), Hangzhou/Shanghai/Shenzhen subsidiaries, and Nanjing Zhihu Information Technology — because they "advance the PRC's military modernization through the development and integration of advanced artificial intelligence research," with a presumption-of-denial license policy ([90 FR 4617](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00704/addition-of-entities-to-and-revision-of-entry-on-the-entity-list); [BIS](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-makes-revisions-entity-list-strengthen-u.s.-national-security); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-adds-16-entities-its-trade-blacklist-14-china-2025-01-15/)). Zhipu "strongly opposes" the designation but has not, on the public record, rebutted it ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/chinese-ai-related-firm-zhipu-says-strongly-opposes-inclusion-us-export-control-2025-01-16/)).
2. **PLA and defense-industry use of Zhipu models.** Recorded Future (June 2025): the PLA and PRC defense industry have very likely used domestic LLMs — including Zhipu AI — to create generative-AI intelligence tools; PLA patent applications reveal methods and systems for AI-facilitated OSINT product generation, intelligence-report drafting, and open-source processing ([Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/artificial-eyes-generative-ai-chinas-military-intelligence)).
3. **The Tsinghua military-civil fusion nexus.** Zhipu's founding lab sits inside the university that is among China's top civilian awardees of AI-related defense contracts ([CSET](https://cset.georgetown.edu/publication/pulling-back-the-curtain-on-chinas-military-civil-fusion/)) and whose leadership has publicly committed to supporting the national military-civil fusion and AI-superpower strategies ([CNAS translation of Tsinghua VP You Zheng](https://www.cnas.org/publications/commentary/tsinghuas-approach-to-military-civil-fusion-in-artificial-intelligence)). The Entity List rationale ("development and integration of advanced AI research") maps directly onto this institutional reality.
4. **PRC government procurement.** Zhipu won 12 of 81 state-sector LLM contracts in H1 2024 — more than any other vendor ([SCMP](https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3267866/chinas-public-sector-accelerates-ai-adoption-2024-zhipu-and-iflytek-emerge-winners); [QQ/骑牛研究所](https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20240626A00GFL00)); a RMB 61.28M Hangzhou municipal deal in May 2025 ([Wikipedia/SCMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)); and a RMB 10.9M China Meteorological Administration contract signed 10 March 2026 for a severe-weather LLM warning platform ([ccgp via 163.com](https://www.163.com/dy/article/KNSSN7E705562DGT.html)). State revenue is structural, not incidental.
5. **Party-state engagement and standards.** Leadership engages Premier Li Qiang; the company plays an active role in setting national AI technical standards ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)).
6. **Digital Silk Road execution.** Sovereign-LLM infrastructure, Huawei "AI-in-a-box," joint innovation centers and national-LLM co-builds across ASEAN, the Gulf, and Africa; Gulf sovereign-capital participation; Huawei Ascend compatibility announced August 2025 ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/openai-says-chinas-zhipu-ai-gaining-ground-amid-beijings-global-ai-push-2025-06-25/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)).
7. **Ecosystem capture.** The RMB 300M "Z Fund" finances open-source AI projects worldwide, explicitly not limited to Zhipu models ([21jingji](https://www.21jingji.com/article/20250418/herald/a0f8f199cdf330c1ab8e6f18e7e586a2.html)) — a subsidy program for dependency formation, run by an Entity-Listed company.

**Assessment.** We assess with high confidence that Zhipu's ties to the PRC state and military ecosystem are definitional rather than incidental, and that "arms-length commercial vendor" is not an available characterization of this company. The open question is not the relationship; it is the operational use Beijing makes of Zhipu's foreign channels — which is precisely where our collection is thinnest (see Intelligence Gaps and the ODNI classified annex).

---

## Data and Access Risk

**Service architecture.** The international Z.ai API is contracted through Jingsheng Hengxing Technology PTE. LTD, 10 Anson Road, Singapore — an affiliate of the PRC parent — while the mainland endpoint (open.bigmodel.cn) hosts data in China ([Z.ai Privacy Policy](https://docs.z.ai/legal-agreement/privacy-policy); [erkinekici comparison](https://erkinekici.com/articles/comparing-llm-api-privacy/)). The Data Processing Addendum for API Services promises no storage of customer content, "processed in Singapore" ([InferCheck GDPR profile](https://infercheck.eu/en/provider/z-ai-coding-plan)). The privacy policy for individual users nonetheless collects account data, device and network information, IP-derived location, usage and browsing history, and logs that may include content present at the time of an error, and reserves the right to use public information to train models ([Z.ai Privacy Policy](https://docs.z.ai/legal-agreement/privacy-policy)).

**Legal compulsion.** PRC National Intelligence Law Art. 7 obliges *all* organizations and citizens to support, assist, and cooperate with state intelligence work; Art. 14 empowers intelligence organs to demand that organizations provide needed support ([NPC text](http://www.npc.gov.cn/zgrdw/npc/xinwen/2017-06/27/content_2024529.htm); [China Law Translate](https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/en/national-intelligence-law-of-the-p-r-c-2017/); [Lawfare](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/beijings-new-national-intelligence-law-defense-offense)). The Cybersecurity Law (Art. 37) imposes localization and state access obligations in the security-review regime. A Singapore-incorporated affiliate cannot contract away its parent's legal obligations; ZDR clauses are marketing, not control.

**What is actually at risk in the hosted channel.** (i) *Prompt content*: approximately 2,300 US-origin organizations are sending prompts to Zhipu-controlled endpoints (case data, low precision) — in the coding-plan product line, that includes source code, repository context, and credentials-bearing configuration files by design ([Z.ai developer docs — coding tools](https://docs.z.ai/scenario-example/develop-tools/others)). (ii) *Identity and metadata*: which US organizations use Zhipu, how much, for what workloads — intelligence value independent of content. (iii) *A continuing service relationship, not a purchase*: hosted model behavior — system prompts, refusals, tool routing, fine-tuning — can be altered server-side at any time by the adversary; "use" of a foreign-controlled model is a live dependency, not a finished good. (iv) *Agentic integration*: GLM Coding Plan and MCP-style integrations give the model standing access to developer environments, files, shell commands, and web search ([Z.ai docs](https://docs.z.ai/scenario-example/develop-tools/others)).

**Open-weights contrast.** Locally-run weights do not, by themselves, exfiltrate data — we have no observed malicious behavior in GLM weights (DHS/CISA input) and no demonstrated covert channel in any released Chinese model ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). The open-weight risk profile is therefore different in kind from the API risk profile — it is technical and structural (next section), not a live data pipe. This distinction should drive channel prioritization: the hosted API is the acute data risk; the weights are the chronic dependency risk.

---

## Open-Weight Distribution Risk

**Scale and license.** GLM-4.5 through GLM-5.3 (753B parameters) are published under a permissive MIT-style license — since 2025 across the family ([Z.ai GLM-5.3 license text](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3/raw/main/LICENSE); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai)) — with Apache 2.0 code on GitHub ([zai-org/GLM-5](https://github.com/zai-org/GLM-5)). The zai-org Hugging Face organization carries >9M cumulative downloads across repositories (case data), with individual GLM-5.x releases in the millions ([Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/zai-org)). MIT terms are perpetual and irrevocable: nothing the USG does retroactively un-licenses files already downloaded, and nothing revokes files already mirrored. Any measure is therefore necessarily forward-looking.

**Technical risks specific to open-weight distribution.**
- *Unverifiable provenance.* No artifact-level method can reconstruct training data, identify an unknown trigger, or prove the absence of poisoning; behavioral testing measures what a model does under known prompts, not what it was built to do ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)).
- *Backdoor/sleeper detection is immature.* White-box detection of sleeper-agent behavior was published only in February 2026 ([Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/04/detecting-backdoored-language-models-at-scale/)) and is not operational at ecosystem scale. DHS/CISA's own assessment (interagency input) is that backdoors and poisoning in open weights are hard to rule out.
- *GLM specifically is under-tested.* DeepSeek received sustained CAISI/METR/Cisco/Qualys scrutiny; GLM entered broad comparative testing only in 2026 and has little model-specific security evidence ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). "No observed malicious behavior" for GLM currently rests on a thin base.
- *No kill switch.* Distribution removes the provider's ability to preserve refusals, monitor use, or withdraw a compromised release ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research), citing UK AISI). Fine-tuning by third parties strips safety training entirely.
- *Update and packaging channels.* Model repositories are living artifacts: config, tokenizer, and code updates distributed alongside weights are an executable supply-chain surface; malicious-client campaigns have already impersonated popular Chinese AI tools ([Anthony West timeline](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)).
- *Benchmark contamination.* Contamination of open benchmarks is demonstrated and detectable only in special cases ([DyePack, EMNLP 2025](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.776)); capability claims for GLM models cannot be independently guaranteed.
- *Agentic deployment.* GLM is marketed specifically for agentic coding and tool use — the deployment pattern in which the model holds shell/file/network access by default ([Z.ai blog](https://z.ai/blog/glm-5.2); [Z.ai GLM-4.5 docs](https://docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-4.5)). DoD's input flags the same concern for DoD networks (interagency input).

**Strategic dimension.** GLM models are trained and served on PRC-domestic silicon (Cambricon; Huawei Ascend compatibility) at costs reported at a small fraction of US equivalents ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai); [WSJ](https://archive.ph/8WgwR)). Beijing has structured this so that US adoption costs Zhipu nothing in restricted inputs while delivering revenue, data, standards influence, and dependency. The open-weight model is the play: it converts an Entity-Listed company into infrastructure.

---

## US Exposure

- **Hosted API:** ~2,300 US-origin organizations observed calling Z.ai endpoints in Q3 2026 (case data; CDN telemetry from a cooperating provider; low precision). Zhipu's global paid base reached ~100,000 monthly API customers plus ~3M free users outside China within two months of the GLM 4.6 launch, with overseas growth exceeding domestic growth ([Asia Daily](https://asiadaily.org/news/9856/)); the company states GLM Coding Plan users are "primarily concentrated in the United States and China" ([Tech Buzz](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/china-s-zhipu-ai-coding-agent-breaks-into-us-developer-market)). Chinese-origin models including GLM 4.6 took seven of the top twenty usage slots on OpenRouter by late 2025, four of the top ten for programming ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2025/11/13/chinas-ai-is-quietly-making-big-inroads-in-silicon-valley)). One US coding platform (Kilo Code) saw token usage rise 94x in twelve days after adding GLM 4.6 ([Asia Daily](https://asiadaily.org/news/9856/)).
- **Open weights:** >9M cumulative downloads (all geographies) of zai-org repositories (case data); served through at least nine US cloud marketplaces and inference providers — e.g., Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita, Parasail, Baseten — several advertising US-based infrastructure, SOC 2, and "zero data retention" for GLM workloads (case data; [Together](https://www.together.ai/models-providers/zai-org); [Fireworks](https://fireworks.ai/models/fireworks/glm-4p6); [DeepInfra](https://deepinfra.com/zai-org/GLM-4.6); [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/glm-4-6-reasoning/providers)).
- **Enterprise integration:** GLM identified in 41 US software products via SBOM sampling — coding assistants, customer-support bots, document processing — of which 6 are federal contractors (case data). GLM output, and possibly GLM-generated code, is therefore plausibly already inside US federal programs through the contractor supply chain, without any federal system having "chosen" a Chinese model. Reporting that US coding-assistant market leaders built products on Chinese models, unconfirmed by the vendors, is consistent with Zhipu's own "internal findings" ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2025/11/13/chinas-ai-is-quietly-making-big-inroads-in-silicon-valley)).
- **Adverse selection effect:** the 12 June 2026 export-control action against US frontier model exports made GLM the least-cost substitute available to US enterprises and developers and visibly accelerated its US adoption ([altpaths](https://altpaths.io/news/3583); [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/06/26/how-zai-is-closing-in-on-americas-ai-frontier.html)). US controls aimed elsewhere are currently Zhipu's best sales team. This is a policy incoherence worth correcting on its own merits.

---

## Mitigation Options / Recommended Measures

Ordered from least to most restrictive; trade-offs stated. Full text of recommendations at [measures.md](./measures.md).

**Option 1 — Monitoring only.** Continue OICTS investigation; obtain the ODNI classified annex; quarterly exposure reporting; CISA advisory. *Pros:* zero economic disruption, preserves open-source norms and security-research access. *Cons:* concedes every channel identified above while GLM compounds into infrastructure; no deterrent; incompatible with an Entity List determination already on the books. **Not recommended as a terminal state.** Retain as the intelligence baseline under any other option.

**Option 2 — Federal-sector prohibition and procurement controls.** CISA/OMB guidance prohibiting Z.ai services and GLM-family use on federal systems; FAR case rule with flow-down to contractors; support for the pending No Adversarial AI Act ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-lawmakers-introduce-bill-bar-chinese-ai-us-government-agencies-2025-06-25/)); department-level device bans in the Commerce/DeepSeek pattern ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/us-commerce-department-bureaus-ban-chinas-deepseek-government-devices-sources-2025-03-17/)); OMB M-25-21/22 implementation ([White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2025/04/white-house-releases-new-policies-on-federal-agency-ai-use-and-procurement/)). *Pros:* immediately implementable; addresses DoD's network concern; closes the 41-products/six-contractors channel for the federal ecosystem. *Cons:* leaves the commercial sector and state/local untouched; depends on enforcement capacity; does not touch the hosted API used by the private sector.

**Option 3 — Entity List consolidation.** ERC action to add the Hong Kong-listed parent (Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC), the Singapore service entity (Jingsheng Hengxing), and post-January 2025 subsidiaries and aliases; Treasury referral for capital-flow and payments screening. *Pros:* closes the rebrand gap and the obvious evasion route; low direct cost. *Cons:* EAR controls exports *to* Zhipu; it does not stop US persons *using* Zhipu services, which are not EAR items. Necessary but not sufficient.

**Option 4 — ICTS determination prohibiting the hosted-API channel.** Determine under 15 CFR 791.7 that US persons' acquisition or use of Zhipu/Z.ai hosted model services (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, coding endpoints) presents an undue risk, and prohibit it. *Pros:* eliminates the acute data channel — the single highest-value exposure (~2,300 organizations) — and is enforceable against identifiable intermediaries: payment rails, US access points, and the service entity's US commercial presence. *Cons:* migration burden for current users; will be litigated; retaliation risk (see below).

**Option 5 — ICTS determination prohibiting US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM weights.** Determine that US-based model hubs, cloud marketplaces, inference providers, and app stores may not distribute, host, serve, or update GLM-family artifacts from Zhipu or its affiliates absent a negotiated mitigation agreement; add takedown and notice duties. *Pros:* this is the enforceable version of "stop the open-weight channel" — it closes the on-ramps (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita, Hugging Face, app stores) rather than chasing individual downloaders; class-based ICTS prohibition has precedent in part 791 itself ([subpart D](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00592/securing-the-information-and-communications-technology-and-services-supply-chain-connected-vehicles)). *Cons:* does not and cannot reach already-downloaded weights or offshore mirrors; will be attacked as an "open-source ban" (it is not — it is a country-of-origin distribution control); some loss of independent security-research access, mitigable by a licensed research carve-out.

**Option 6 — Negotiated mitigation in lieu of prohibition, for intermediaries only.** Where a US intermediary can demonstrate independent control — verified provenance, third-party artifact scanning, AIBOM disclosure, country-of-origin labeling, takedown obligations — permit continued serving under revocable conditions. *Pros:* preserves US infrastructure choices and the research carve-out while transferring compliance cost to the distributor. *Cons:* verification technology is immature (see KJ-5); risk of becoming a paper regime; should be the exception, not the default.

**Option 7 — Total prohibition, including private self-hosted use.** Prohibit US persons' possession/use of GLM weights outright. *Pros:* maximal coverage on paper. *Cons:* unenforceable against private servers and offline copies; would be the first US ban on mere possession of software weights; maximal retaliation and precedent risk; State/EB's objections (interagency input) are correct here. **Not recommended.**

**RECOMMENDED PACKAGE (decisive, enforceable):** Options 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 immediately, with Option 6 available as a narrow, revocable exception, and Option 1 retained as the monitoring baseline. Rationale: every dollar of GLM adoption in the US is revenue, data, and standards influence for an Entity-Listed instrument of PRC military modernization, and each month of delay entrenches it. The package is calibrated to *enforceability*, not to the severity of the threat — which is why private, offline self-hosting is deferred rather than exempted. Recommended measures in detail: [measures.md](./measures.md).

**Enforceability analysis (State/EB's request, interagency input).** Three points. First, §791.1's "use" prong supplies authority over US-person use of services; enforcement is then a matter of *where* the government can observe and compel — intermediaries (hubs, marketplaces, inference providers, app stores, payment processors) are US persons with US nexus and are identifiable; individual offline users are not. Second, precedent exists for class-based prohibition without individual-possession enforcement: the connected-vehicles rule ([15 CFR 791 subpart D](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/16/2025-00592/securing-the-information-and-communications-technology-and-services-supply-chain-connected-vehicles)) prohibits classes of transactions through import/sale channels, not the possession of already-sold cars. Third, private self-hosted use should be addressed where it is *visible and governable*: federal procurement flow-down (Option 2), critical-infrastructure regulation (NERC, financial, health-sector regulators), and disclosure duties (Option 6-style AIBOM requirements) — rather than by a criminal prohibition the government cannot police.

**Reciprocity and retaliation (State/EB).** PRC retaliation is a real cost but not a new one: Beijing already excludes US models and US hardware from state procurement, and US firms with major PRC exposure (Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, US AI labs' partners) are already exposed. The measures above take aim at *channels*, not at PRC persons generally, and mirror restrictions Beijing already imposes on US ICTS. We assess the marginal retaliation risk of Options 2–5 as low to moderate, and the strategic cost of inaction as high: the PRC's stated objective — captured in Zhipu's own positioning — is to lock Chinese AI systems and standards into as many markets as possible before the West organizes ([OpenAI Global Affairs](https://openaiglobalaffairs.substack.com/p/chinese-progress-at-the-front)).

---

## Intelligence Gaps

1. **Covert content of GLM weights.** We cannot confirm or rule out trigger-conditioned behaviors, poisoning, or sleeper constructs in any GLM release with existing methods; GLM-specific deep evaluation is thinner than DeepSeek's ([Anthony West](https://anthonywest.co.uk/research/chinese-model-security-research)). This gap is not closeable by analysis; it requires sustained artifact research (recommend funding a NIST/CAISI GLM evaluation).
2. **Actual data flows of the hosted channel.** No visibility into whether US-person API traffic is wholly processed in Singapore or transits mainland infrastructure; no visibility into PRC state requests to Zhipu or its affiliates. The ODNI classified annex (available on request; not in this enclave) may partially address this.
3. **Zhipu–PLA operational nexus.** The ERC determination and Recorded Future's assessment establish the military-modernization link; specific projects, contracts, or tasking involving Zhipu models in PLA systems are not visible in open sources.
4. **Hong Kong/Singapore structure.** Full shareholder table and control chain of the listed parent (including any post-IPO state-linked stakes) requires the HKEX prospectus and Treasury analysis; Treasury/OIA input is still pending (interagency input).
5. **Exposure precision.** The ~2,300-organization estimate is low-precision CDN telemetry; the identity of the 41 US products and the six federal contractors, and what data those products transmit, remain unenumerated (case data). SBOM sampling does not capture silent dependencies.
6. **US institutional capital exposure.** US persons can and likely do hold SEHK 2513 shares; scale unknown.
7. **PRC retaliation planning and allied positions.** No collection reflected in this product; State/EB and ODNI inputs needed before final decision.
8. **Update-channel telemetry.** No visibility into how often GLM repositories issue config/tokenizer/code updates to already-downloaded weights, or who consumes them.
