# ICTS CASE 2026-0412 — RECOMMENDED MEASURES
**CUI//PROPIN**

**Subject:** Zhipu AI (Beijing Zhipu Huazhang Technology Co., Ltd., d/b/a Z.ai; HK-listed Knowledge Atlas Technology JSC, SEHK 2513) — GLM-family models
**Companion product:** OICTS Assessment, ICTS Case 2026-0412 ([assessment.md](./assessment.md))
**Authority:** E.O. 13873, as amended; 15 CFR part 791 (§§ 791.1, 791.7, 791.100–110); Entity List per 15 CFR 744, supplement no. 4; IEEPA authorities delegated to the Secretary
**Recommendation:** Adopt measures M2–M6 immediately as a package; retain M1 and M7–M9 as the supporting baseline. Do not adopt M-limitless (blanket possession ban) — see final paragraph. Analysts draft; the Executive Director and Under Secretary decide.

---

**M1. Monitoring and intelligence baseline (retain under all options).** OICTS keeps Case 2026-0412 open, obtains the ODNI classified annex, and stands up quarterly reporting on GLM/Z.ai US exposure (API call volume by sector, marketplace availability, new GLM releases, enterprise-integration discoveries via SBOM sampling), while DHS/CISA issues a public advisory to critical-infrastructure operators describing the risk classes of foreign-adversary-derived AI models. Trade-off: this is the floor, not the policy — it preserves visibility and open-source research access at zero economic cost but changes nothing about the channels themselves, and GLM compounds into US infrastructure while we watch. Recommended as the intelligence baseline that runs underneath every other measure, not as a terminal response.

**M2. Federal-sector prohibition with contractor flow-down (implement immediately).** CISA and OMB issue guidance prohibiting the acquisition or use of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family models (hosted, marketplace, or self-hosted) on federal information systems, including government-furnished equipment, in the pattern already set by the DeepSeek device bans; OMB ties the restriction into M-25-21/22 implementation; a FAR case rule (with DFARS companion) prohibits foreign-adversary-derived AI components in contractor deliverables to USG, closing the "41 US products / six federal contractors" channel; DoD issues a service-wide direction on open weights per OUSD(I&S)'s input, covering downloaded weights on DoD networks and personally owned devices used for DoD work; OICTS supports pending No Adversarial AI Act legislation. Trade-off: immediately implementable and near-zero litigation risk for the government-use prong, but it protects only the federal ecosystem — the 2,300-organization commercial exposure and the general developer market remain untouched, and the FAR rule needs a rulemaking cycle.

**M3. Entity List consolidation — close the rebrand and evasion gaps (implement immediately).** Refer to the ERC additions of (i) Knowledge Atlas Technology Joint Stock Company Limited (the HK-listed parent, SEHK 2513), (ii) Jingsheng Hengxing Technology PTE. LTD (Singapore, the international service front), and (iii) all post-January-2025 subsidiaries and aliases (e.g., Zhejiang Zhipu Xinbian, the February 2025 Hangzhou subsidiary), under the same §744.11 military-modernization basis and presumption of denial as the ten existing entries; refer to Treasury for analysis of US institutional holdings in SEHK 2513 and for payments screening of the Singapore entity. Trade-off: low cost and closes the most obvious evasion route (the 2025 rebrand and the Singapore front were almost certainly built for this purpose), but Entity List controls the flow of items *to* Zhipu — they do not stop US persons *using* Zhipu services, since services are not EAR items. Necessary, not sufficient.

**M4. ICTS determination: prohibit US-person transactions involving Zhipu-hosted model services (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a §791.7 determination that the acquisition or use by US persons of hosted model services from Zhipu, Z.ai, or affiliates (api.z.ai, open.bigmodel.cn, api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4, and successor endpoints) presents an undue risk to US national security, and prohibits those transactions, with enforcement directed at identifiable intermediaries — payment processors, US access points, the service entities' US commercial presence — rather than at individual subscribers, and with a 60–90 day wind-down for current subscribers to migrate. Trade-off: this closes the acute channel through which ~2,300 US-origin organizations are sending prompts, source code, and business documents to an Entity-Listed, intelligence-law-subject vendor; it will draw litigation (the IEEPA record under part 791 is strong but untested on AI services), imposes real migration costs on current users, and carries retaliation risk — none of which changes the underlying fact that this channel is the single highest-value exposure in the case.

**M5. ICTS determination: prohibit US intermediary distribution/servicing of GLM open weights, absent negotiated mitigation (implement immediately).** OICTS prepares a companion class-based determination that US persons may not distribute, host, serve, market, update, or otherwise deal in GLM-family artifacts originating from Zhipu or its affiliates — model hubs (e.g., the zai-org organization on Hugging Face), cloud marketplaces and inference providers (Together, Fireworks, DeepInfra, Novita, Parasail, Baseten, OpenRouter-listed providers, and successors), and app stores for Z.ai applications — without an approved mitigation agreement, with takedown and user-notice obligations attached. This is deliberately aimed at the on-ramps, not at possession: files already downloaded remain where they are, offline mirrors remain outside US jurisdiction, and no individual is penalized for a past download. Trade-off: enforceable because every named intermediary is a US person with US nexus, and class-based prohibition has precedent in part 791 itself (the connected-vehicles rule); but it cannot reach what is already in the wild, it will be attacked rhetorically as "an open-source ban" (it is a country-of-origin distribution control on one vendor's artifacts), and it costs the United States some independent security-research visibility into GLM — mitigated by the M6 carve-out.

**M6. Narrow, revocable mitigation exception for intermediaries and researchers (adopt alongside M4–M5).** Where a US intermediary or an accredited research institution can demonstrate independent control — verified provenance and checksummed release lineage, third-party artifact scanning under the emerging white-box methods, AI bill-of-materials (AIBOM) disclosure, country-of-origin labeling in model cards and SBOMs, defined takedown obligations, and no commercial relationship with Zhipu or its affiliates — OICTS may permit continued hosting or research use under written conditions revocable at any time. Trade-off: preserves US infrastructure choice, keeps the research carve-out that makes M5 defensible, and transfers compliance cost to the distributor; the risk is that verification technology is immature (artifact methods cannot prove absence of poisoning today), so conditions must be treated as provisional and reviewed quarterly, and the exception must remain narrow enough that it does not become a paper regime.

**M7. Disclosure and labeling duties for the enterprise-integration channel (implement immediately).** Commerce (OICTS with NIST) publishes a requirement — first as guidance, then by rulemaking — that vendors of software and AI-enabled services sold in the US disclose foreign-adversary-derived model components (base or fine-tune) in AIBOMs/SBOMs, with specific mandatory disclosure to federal buyers and to critical-infrastructure customers, enforced by FTC/Commerce against undisclosed use; buyers' contracts should require flow-down of the same disclosure. Trade-off: this is the only tool that reaches the quiet channel — GLM embedded in products whose buyers never chose a Chinese model — and it is cheap and standards-friendly; its limits are that disclosure is not prohibition, enforcement against a disclosure failure is after the fact, and it depends on vendor honesty absent audit.

**M8. Critical-infrastructure and sector-regulator actions (implement on the same schedule as M2).** Sector regulators and CISA advise — and where statutory authority exists, require — the exclusion of Zhipu/Z.ai services and GLM-family self-hosted deployments from systems that operate or are connected to critical infrastructure (energy, financial services, water, communications, healthcare), in line with CISA's supply-chain concern that open-weight backdoors and poisoning cannot be ruled out; regulators (FERC/NERC, financial regulators, HHS) incorporate the prohibition into their inspection regimes. Trade-off: this is where private self-hosted use is both visible and governable, so it substitutes for an unenforceable blanket ban (see below) without leaving a gap for the highest-consequence deployments; the cost is regulator-by-regulator implementation time and compliance burden on operators.

**M9. Allied engagement and retaliation contingency (State/EB lead; begin now).** State briefs allies and partner governments on the Zhipu case file — sovereign-AI customers along the Belt and Road are the intended audience of our evidence on Huawei-based "AI-in-a-box," joint innovation centers, and standards capture — and coordinates reciprocal measures; Treasury, Commerce, and USTR jointly model and prepare mitigation for PRC retaliation against US firms with China exposure (Apple, Tesla, Microsoft, US AI labs' partners), including export-licensing flexibility and market-access remedies. Trade-off: early engagement raises the cost of Beijing flipping our measures into a "tech hegemony" narrative and multiplies the effect by closing third markets to Zhipu's sovereign-AI play; the risk is that allies move at different speeds and leaks complicate the interagency process. Not doing it concedes the third-world standards contest that is the actual prize.

**Not recommended: a blanket prohibition on possession or private offline use of GLM weights.** State/EB's objection is sustained: such a ban would be novel (the first US prohibition on mere possession of software), unenforceable against private servers, offshore mirrors, and already-downloaded files, and maximally provocative, and it would undercut the enforceable architecture above by attaching the whole policy to its weakest link. The recommended package (M2–M6, with M7–M9 in support) covers every channel that the US Government can actually see and compel — hosted services, distribution intermediaries, federal procurement, critical infrastructure, and disclosure — which is where the risk actually lives.
